title: An Extraordinary Escape
blurb: Tell a more complex past story

steps.html:
In 1849 a man in Virginia had himself nailed into a wooden box and posted to Pennsylvania. The story only works if you can move between two moments in the past at once — which is exactly what this lesson's grammar is for.

  • Read the same escape from two points of view
  • Use the past perfect, simple and continuous, active and passive
  • Use precise adjectives for strong feelings
  • Write a story that moves between two past moments

steps.title: Study the words.

words.def: Worried about something that might happen.

Unable to tell where you are or which way you are facing.
So frightened that you cannot move. Stronger than terrified.
Unable to understand something; confused by it.
Glad because something you feared did not happen.
Unhappy and disturbed; to make someone feel that way.
Nervous, and unable to relax, because of what may happen next.
The system in which people are owned by other people.
What someone leaves behind them — work, influence, or an example.
To make certain that something happens.
To examine something carefully in order to find out the truth.

steps.title: Twenty-seven hours in a wooden crate
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 148 words

Henry Brown was born into slavery in Virginia in 1815. He had worked in a tobacco factory since he was fifteen, and by 1848 he had married and had three children. That year his owner sold his wife and children to a plantation in another state. Brown had done nothing to deserve it, and he could do nothing to stop it.

He was furious, then bitter, and then determined. He asked a friend, a carpenter, to build him a wooden crate about a metre long. On 23 March 1849 he climbed in with a bag of water and a few biscuits, and two friends nailed the lid shut.

The box went by wagon, by railway and by steamboat. For part of the way it had been loaded upside down. Brown, who had been folded into it for twenty-seven hours, was miserable, anxious and, for one long stretch, petrified.

steps.title: What made Brown decide to escape?
options: He had been promised his freedom and it was refused.
His wife and children were sold to another state.
He had been moved to a harder job in the factory.
steps.answer: His wife and children were sold to another state.
steps.why: 'That year his owner sold his wife and children to a plantation in another state.'

steps.title: Look at the order of the feelings.
steps.sub: 'He was furious, then bitter, and then determined.'
steps.prompt: What is the writer showing with that sequence?
options: That his feelings were confused and changed at random.
That the anger cooled into something lasting, and then into a plan.
That he regretted his decision almost immediately.

steps.why: Furious is the moment, bitter is what remains, determined is what he did with it. The order is the argument.

steps.title: The room where the box was opened
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 146 words

In Philadelphia four men were waiting for a package from Virginia. They had been told to expect it on the 24th, and by the time it arrived they were tense enough to have stopped speaking to one another. One of them tapped on the lid and asked whether everything was all right inside.

A voice said that it was. The men, who had been terrified that they were about to open a coffin, were so relieved that one of them had to sit down.

Brown climbed out disorientated, unable to stand, and delighted. The handlers along the route would have been puzzled if they had heard anything at all; nobody had. He became famous as Henry 'Box' Brown, and his legacy is not only the escape itself but the account he wrote of it afterwards, which upset a great many people who had preferred not to know.

steps.title: Reaching back from a point in the past
steps.html:
The full picture: simple, continuous, active, passive — and when not to use it.

A story stands at some moment in the past. When you need to reach back to something that happened before that moment, you use the past perfect: had + past participle.

By 1848 he had married and had three children. The story's moment is 1848; the marriage came earlier. The form is the same for every subject — had never changes.

The past perfect continuous — had been + -ing — does the same job for something that was going on for a period before that moment: He had been folded into the box for twenty-seven hours. It answers how long.

It has a passive too: had been + past participle. For part of the way it had been loaded upside down.

Do not use it for every past event. If the events are told in the order they happened, the past simple is enough: He climbed in, they nailed the lid, the box left. The past perfect is only for stepping backwards out of that order.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences, all from the two texts.

He had worked in a tobacco factory since he was fifteen.
Earlier than 1848, the story's moment.

By 1848 he had married and had three children.
By + a past date almost always pulls the past perfect.

Brown had done nothing to deserve it.
Negative past perfect.

For part of the way it had been loaded upside down.
Past perfect passive.

He had been folded into it for twenty-seven hours.
Passive, and it answers how long.

They had been told to expect it on the 24th.
Passive; the telling came before the waiting.

They had been terrified that they were opening a coffin.
A state that existed before the box was opened.

The handlers would have been puzzled if they had heard anything.
Past perfect in a third conditional clause.

Nobody had.
The whole verb phrase reduced to had — very natural in English.

It upset people who had preferred not to know.
Their preference existed before the account appeared.

He climbed in and they nailed the lid shut.
In sequence, so past simple — no past perfect needed.

The box went by wagon, by railway and by steamboat.
Also in sequence. Past simple.

steps.title: Deciding whether you need the past perfect at all
steps.html:
1. Two facts: (1) the friends nailed the lid shut; (2) Brown climbed into the box.
  2. Ask: am I telling them in the order they happened? Yes — he climbed in, then they nailed it. So both stay in the past simple: He climbed in and they nailed the lid shut.
  3. Now change the order for effect: They nailed the lid shut. He had climbed in an hour earlier. Because the second sentence steps backwards, it needs the past perfect.
  4. If the point is how long something lasted before that moment, use the continuous: He had been sitting in the box for an hour before they nailed it.
  5. And if the subject did not do the action, use the passive: The box had been nailed shut before it left the house.

steps.title: You are going to write a story that moves between two moments in the past.

options.label: A journey where something had already gone wrong before you set off
A day you arrived somewhere and found things had changed
A time you found out something that had been kept from you
A moment you had been waiting a long time for

steps.title: Write your story.
steps.sub: 150–180 words. Use the past perfect at least four times, and at least once in the continuous or the passive.
steps.html:
• Open at the main moment, in the past simple.
  • Step backwards with the past perfect: what had already happened.
  • Use the past perfect continuous once, for how long something had gone on.
  • Use the past perfect passive once, for something done by someone else.
  • Close in the present, looking back.

Useful language

  • By the time I arrived, …
  • I had been …-ing for … when …
  • Nobody had told me that …
  • It had already been decided that …
  • I found out later that they had …
  • Looking back, I had never really believed that …
steps.modelHtml:
The flat on Kirov Street

I got the keys on a Thursday in October. I had been waiting for that flat since March, and by the time the agency finally called, I had almost stopped believing it would happen.

What nobody had told me was that the previous tenant had left in August. The heating had been switched off at the mains, the lift had been out of service for six weeks, and somebody had taken the door of the kitchen cupboard away without replacing it.

I stood in the hallway for a long time. I was not furious, exactly. I was disorientated: I had built a picture of this flat over seven months and I was now standing inside a different one.

I lived there for four years and I was very happy. But I have never quite forgiven that cupboard door.
